t.3.10.1: Rāma went on ahead, slender-waisted Sītā walked in the middle, and behind them followed Lakṣmaṇa, bow in hand.
t.3.10.3: They saw cranes and cakravāka birds roaming the sandbanks of the rivers, and lakes full of lotuses, thronged with water-born birds.
t.3.10.2: Those two went on together with Sītā, beholding many kinds of mountain plateaus and forests, and various delightful rivers.
t.3.10.4: Spotted deer bound together in herds, horned beasts frenzied with rut, buffaloes and boars, and elephants, the foes of trees.
t.3.10.5: Having travelled a long way, when the sun was sinking low, they together beheld a lovely lake, a yojana in length.
t.3.10.6: It was thick with lotuses and lilies and adorned with herds of elephants, teeming with sārasa cranes, swans, kādamba geese and other creatures that move upon the water.
t.3.10.7: From that lovely lake with its clear waters there was heard the sound of singing and of musical instruments, yet no one at all could be seen.
t.3.10.8: Then, out of curiosity, Rāma and the great chariot-warrior Lakṣmaṇa began to question the sage named Dharmabhṛt.
t.3.10.9: O great sage, having heard this most wondrous thing, a great curiosity has arisen in all of us. What is this? Let it be properly told.
t.3.10.10: Thus addressed by Rāghava, the righteous sage then began to relate in full the wondrous power of the lake.
t.3.10.11: O Rāma, this lake, named Pañcāpsaras, which endures through all seasons, was created through the power of his austerity by the sage Māṇḍakarṇi.
t.3.10.12: For that great sage Māṇḍakarṇi practised fierce austerity for ten thousand years, living on air alone and dwelling in the water.
t.3.10.13: Then all the gods, with Agni at their head, greatly alarmed, gathered together and all spoke these words to one another: "This sage seeks the position of one of us."
t.3.10.14: Then five foremost apsarases, whose radiance flickered like lightning, were appointed by all the gods to create an obstacle to his austerity.
t.3.10.15: Then by those apsarases the sage, who had seen the higher and the lower, was brought under the sway of Madana, for the accomplishment of the gods' purpose.
t.3.10.16: And those five Apsarases became the wives of the sage; within this lake a hidden dwelling was built for them.
t.3.10.17: There indeed five Apsarases dwell at their ease and delight the sage, who through the power of his austerities has attained youth.
t.3.10.18: Of those women as they sport together, this sound of musical instruments is heard, and the charming sound of singing, mingled with the jingling of ornaments.
t.3.10.19: Exclaiming “Wonderful!”, the greatly renowned Rāghava, together with his brother, received these words of that pure-souled one.
t.3.10.20: While he was speaking thus, he saw the circle of hermitages, strewn with kuśa grass and bark garments and surrounded by many kinds of trees.
t.3.10.22: Having dwelt there very happily, honored by the great seers, he went in turn to the hermitages of those ascetics.
t.3.10.21: Then Rāghava, that Kākutstha, having entered that splendid circle of hermitages together with Vaidehī and Lakṣmaṇa, there…
t.3.10.23: In whose presence that great master of weapons had formerly dwelt, staying in some places for some ten months and in others for a single year.
t.3.10.24: In one place he stayed four months, in others five or six, elsewhere still more months, and in yet another place a month and a half longer.
t.3.10.26: And having wandered about, the glorious Rāghava, knower of dharma, came back once again with Sītā to the hermitage of Sutīkṣṇa.
t.3.10.25: Rāghava dwelt happily, for three months in one place and for eight months in another. And as he thus lived in the hermitages of the sages, delighting in their kindness, ten years passed by.
t.3.10.27: Having come to that hermitage and been honored by the sages, Rāma, the tamer of foes, dwelt there too for some time.
t.3.10.28: Then once, while staying at the hermitage and humbly attending upon that great sage Sutīkṣṇa, Kākutstha spoke these words to him.
t.3.10.29: O blessed one, I have always heard from those who tell tales that Agastya, the best of sages, dwells in this forest.
t.3.10.30: But because of the vastness of this forest I do not know that place, where the holy hermitage of that wise great sage lies.
t.3.10.31: By the grace of your honored self, may I, together with my younger brother and with Sītā, go to the sage Agastya to pay my respects to him.
t.3.10.32: This great wish keeps turning over in my heart: that I might myself attend upon and serve that foremost of sages.
t.3.10.33: Having heard these words of the righteous-souled Rāma, the sage Sutīkṣṇa, delighted, replied thus to the son of Daśaratha.
t.3.10.34: I too was wishing to say this very thing to you and Lakṣmaṇa: go to Agastya together with Sītā, O Rāghava.
t.3.10.36: Go, dear son, four yojanas from this āśrama; then, to the south, lies the great and splendid āśrama of Agastya's brother.
t.3.10.35: Fortunately, now you yourself speak to me about this very matter. I tell you, dear child, where the great sage Agastya is.
t.3.10.37: In a forest region of mostly level ground, adorned with groves of pippalī, delightful, rich in flowers and fruits, and resounding with the cries of many kinds of birds.
t.3.10.38: There were lotus ponds of many kinds, auspicious and with clear water, crowded with haṃsas and kāraṇḍava ducks and adorned with cakravāka birds.
t.3.10.39: Having spent one night there, O Rāma, set out at daybreak, taking the southern direction along the edge of the forest grove.
t.3.10.40: Going on from there a further distance of one yojana to the hermitage of Agastya, in a delightful stretch of forest covered with many trees, Vaidehī will take delight there, and Lakṣmaṇa too, together with you.
t.3.10.41: That stretch of forest is indeed delightful, thick with many trees. If you have resolved to see Agastya, that great sage, then set your mind on going this very day, O greatly renowned one.
t.3.10.42: Having thus heard the sage's words, Rāma, together with his brother, saluted him, and then set out toward Agastya, accompanied by his younger brother and by Sītā.
t.3.10.43: Gazing on the many-hued forests, on mountains like masses of cloud, on lakes and on rivers along the way, they went on, following wherever the path led them.
t.3.10.44: Having gone comfortably along that path pointed out by Sutīkṣṇa, he, supremely delighted, spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa.
t.3.10.45: This, surely, is the hermitage that is seen here, belonging to that great-souled brother of the sage Agastya, whose deeds are holy.
t.3.10.47: And this fragrance of ripe pippalī berries, borne aloft by the wind, has suddenly come to us from this forest, rising pungent and sharp.
t.3.10.46: For just as these trees of this forest, known by the thousands along the path, stand bowed down under the weight of their fruit and the weight of their flowers…
t.3.10.48: Here and there heaps of firewood are seen gathered together, and along the path are seen cut darbha grasses gleaming like beryl.
t.3.10.49: And here, standing in the midst of the forest, is seen the plume of smoke from the fire that dwells in the hermitage, resembling the peak of a dark cloud.
t.3.10.50: And at secluded bathing places, the twice-born, having bathed, make offerings of flowers with blossoms they have gathered themselves.
t.3.10.51: O gentle one, according to the words of Sutīkṣṇa as I heard them, this must surely be the hermitage of Agastya's brother.
t.3.10.53: Here once, it is said, there lived together two brothers, the cruel Vātāpi and Ilvala, mighty asuras who were slayers of brāhmaṇas.
t.3.10.52: He whose brother, a man of virtuous deeds, forcibly subdued death out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds and made this region a place of refuge.
t.3.10.54: Assuming the form of a brāhmaṇa and speaking refined Sanskrit, that pitiless Ilvala invites the brāhmaṇas, ostensibly for a śrāddha ceremony.
t.3.10.55: Then the brother, by the rite prescribed for the śrāddha, fed those twice-born the brother who had taken the form of a ram, once he had been prepared.
t.3.10.56: Then, when those brahmins had eaten, Ilvala spoke, calling out in a loud voice, "Vātāpi, come out!"
t.3.10.57: Then, hearing his brother's words, Vātāpi, bleating like a ram, burst forth again and again, tearing apart the bodies of the brāhmaṇas.
t.3.10.58: Thousands of brāhmaṇas have thus been destroyed by those flesh-eaters, who assume any form at will, banding together and attacking constantly.
t.3.10.59: Then, it is said, that great asura was devoured at a śrāddha by the great sage Agastya, who had been entreated by the gods and who partook of him there.
t.3.10.60: Then, having said, "It is complete," and having given water for washing the hands, Ilvala called out to his brother, "Come out!"
t.3.10.61: But as that brother, the slayer of brahmins, was speaking thus, the wise Agastya, best of sages, laughed and said to him:
t.3.10.62: How could the rākṣasa, your brother who took the form of a ram, digested by me and gone to the abode of Yama, have the power to come out?
t.3.10.63: Then, having heard his words concerning the death of his brother, the night-wanderer in fury began to assail the sage.
t.3.10.64: He rushed at that foremost of the twice-born, and, burned up by the sage of blazing splendor with an eye like fire, he met his death.
t.3.10.65: This is the hermitage of that brother, adorned with ponds and woods, by whom, out of compassion for the brahmins, this difficult deed was accomplished.
t.3.10.66: While Rāma was speaking thus with Saumitri, the sun went to its setting, and the time of evening twilight came on.
t.3.10.68: Rāghava, duly received by that sage, ate roots and fruits and stayed there for that one night.
t.3.10.67: Having performed the evening twilight worship according to the prescribed rite together with his brother, he entered the hermitage, and they respectfully saluted that sage.
t.3.10.69: When that night had passed and the orb of the sun shone clear, Rāghava took leave of that brother of Agastya.
t.3.10.71: Told by him, "Let it be gone," Raghunandana went by the path as it had been pointed out, gazing upon that forest as he went.
t.3.10.70: I salute you, venerable one; I have passed the night happily. I take leave of you and go to see your elder brother, the teacher.
t.3.10.73: There Rāma saw hundreds of forest trees in full bloom, entwined by creepers whose tips were laden with flowers.
t.3.10.72: Nīvāra, panasa, tāla, timiśa, vañjula and dhava trees, ciribilvas and madhūkas, and also bilvas and tindukas.
t.3.10.75: Then lotus-eyed Rāma spoke to the heroic Lakṣmaṇa, enhancer of prosperity, who stood close by, following behind him.
t.3.10.74: The trees were crushed by the trunks of elephants and adorned with monkeys, and they echoed with the cries of hundreds of flocks of impassioned birds.
t.3.10.76: Judging by how the trees have glossy leaves and how tranquil the beasts and birds are, the hermitage of the great sage of purified soul cannot be far away.
t.3.10.77: Renowned in the world as Agastya by virtue of his own deeds, his hermitage is seen here, a place that dispels the weariness of the exhausted.
t.3.10.78: Its woods are thick with abundant smoke, and it is adorned with rows of bark garments; its herds of deer are tranquil, and it resounds with the calls of many kinds of birds.
t.3.10.79: He of meritorious deeds, by whom, having forcibly restrained Death out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, the southern quarter was made a place of refuge.
t.3.10.80: This is the hermitage of him through whose power this southern region is only looked upon by the rākṣasas out of fear, and is not enjoyed by them.
t.3.10.81: And ever since this region was occupied by that sage of meritorious deeds, from that time on the night-roaming demons have been at peace, free of hostility.
t.3.10.82: By the name of the blessed one, this auspicious southern direction is renowned throughout the three worlds and cannot be assailed by those of cruel deeds.
t.3.10.84: This is the splendid hermitage of that long-lived Agastya, whose deeds are renowned in the world, a place frequented by tame deer.
t.3.10.83: Heeding his command, the Vindhya mountain, best of peaks, does not grow to block forever the path of the sun.
t.3.10.85: He is a holy man honored by the world, ever devoted to the welfare of the virtuous. Now that we have come to him, he will bestow on us what is good.
t.3.10.86: Here I shall honour that great sage Agastya, and here, gentle one, O lord, I shall spend the remainder of my forest exile.
t.3.10.87: Here the gods together with the Gandharvas, the Siddhas and the supreme sages constantly attend upon Agastya, who is restrained in his diet.
t.3.10.88: No liar could live here, nor anyone cruel or deceitful, nor one who is wicked or driven by lust; such is the nature of this sage.
t.3.10.89: Here the gods, the Yakṣas and the Nāgas, together with the birds, dwell with restrained diet, eager to propitiate dharma.
t.3.10.90: Here great-souled supreme seers, having attained perfection, cast off their bodies and went to heaven in new bodies, borne on celestial chariots shining like the sun.
t.3.10.91: Here the gods, when worshipped by virtuous beings, bestow the state of a Yakṣa, immortality, and kingdoms of various kinds.
t.3.10.92: We have arrived at the hermitage, O Saumitri; go in ahead and announce to the sage that I have come here together with Sītā.
